sources.title: Alexander Kleshchev, Lectures on Infinite Dimensional Lie Algebras
sources.locator: Local complete PDF/text inspected: printed pp.10--42, 50--60, 68--76, 116--118, 122--126. Remote full-body verification is recorded in fetch_verified; the original DNS failures are historical. Sections 1.2--1.5, 2, 3.1--3.2, 4.1--4.2, 5, 9.1 and 9.3; individual results below narrow uses.

contents.name: Kleshchev §1.2, pp.10--12
contents.support: Fix a nonempty finite index set {1,...,n} and integer entries; all diagonal entries are 2, off-diagonal entries nonpositive, and the zero pattern is symmetric. Define indecomposable by absence of a nontrivial block partition.

contents.name: Kleshchev §2.1, pp.26--29
contents.support: Fix positive rational d_i with d_i a_ij=d_j a_ji, scaling to integers componentwise if desired. Prove rational normalization by propagating the positive ratios along a finite spanning tree; cycle consistency follows from the supplied symmetrizer. Translate Kleshchev A=diag(epsilon_i)B by d_i=1/epsilon_i, not by d_i=epsilon_i.

contents.name: Kleshchev Definition 1.2.2, pp.10--11
contents.support: Work over C; h_i and alpha_i are each independent, alpha_j(h_i)=a_ij and dim h=2n-rank A. An isomorphism preserves both indexed families; it need not be unique.

contents.name: Kleshchev Proposition 1.2.4, pp.11--12
contents.support: Use the rank-r pairing of the coroot span with the simple-root span. Extend its row and column spaces separately to obtain independent roots and coroots on a (2n-r)-space; use independent row/column rank pivots, not the unjustified assertion that a general nonsymmetric A has a nonsingular principal rank minor. For uniqueness compare kernels of the map h -> C^n, choose finite complements, and change complementary coordinates by the coroot span. The resulting linear isomorphism preserves both families. Finite linear elimination adds no AC.

contents.name: Kleshchev §1.3, pp.13--16
contents.support: Take the free Lie algebra on a fixed finite basis of h and e_i,f_i, quotient by [h,hprime]=0, [h,e_i]=alpha_i(h)e_i, [h,f_i]=-alpha_i(h)f_i, [e_i,f_j]=delta_ij h_i. State the quotient universal property. Cartan injectivity and freeness of the halves are obligations supplied next, not assumptions.

contents.name: Kleshchev Theorem 1.3.3, pp.13--16
contents.support: Use T(C^n) with f_i acting by left concatenation; h on a word has eigenvalue lambda minus its root sum; recursively e_i(f_j a)=delta_ij h_i(a)+f_j e_i(a). Check all four relation families by word-length induction. Evaluation on 1 for every lambda proves Cartan injectivity and independence of the negative half; the involution e_i -> -f_i, f_i -> -e_i, h -> -h supplies the other half. Reordering mixed brackets by Jacobi proves spanning. The embedding of each free half into its tensor algebra proves freeness. State the Q-grading and the finite word bound at each height.

contents.name: Kleshchev Lemma 1.3.2 and Theorem 1.3.3, pp.13--16
contents.support: For any ideal and each vector with finite weight support, choose h separating those finitely many weights and apply Lagrange interpolation polynomials in ad h to extract every component. Thus every ideal is graded, not merely ideals declared graded. The zero component of every ideal disjoint from h is zero, and remains zero in their arbitrary algebraic sum. Show the positive and negative intersections are separate ideals using [f_i,nplus] subset nplus+h and zero Cartan intersection. This constructs the largest ideal r without Zorn or AC.

contents.name: Kleshchev §1.4, pp.16--19
contents.support: Define g(A)=gtilde/r using the proved largest ideal. Transport h, e_i, f_i and the sign-changing involution. Any nonzero ideal of g has nonzero intersection with h, by taking its inverse image; do not confuse this property with simplicity.

contents.name: Kleshchev Theorem 1.3.3 and §1.4, pp.13--19
contents.support: Quotient the homogeneous decomposition. At height m the half is spanned by finitely many iterated brackets in n generators; dim g_alpha <= n^m. The only pure simple-root degrees are plus/minus alpha_i, each one-dimensional, because [e_i,e_i]=0 and h_i=[e_i,f_i] is nonzero. Every nonzero root has one sign. Include that a simple reflection can change a positive root to negative only for alpha_i once its image is known to be a root.

contents.name: Kleshchev §§2.1--2.2, Theorem 2.2.3, pp.26--32
contents.support: Normalize (h_i,h)=alpha_i(h)/d_i and (e_i,f_j)=delta_ij/d_i. Fix a finite complement to the coroot span and set its self-pairing zero. Prove nondegeneracy on h: the annihilator of all simple roots lies in the coroot span, whose radical has dimension n-r; then root independence kills a vector in the full radical. Extend the form by height, setting unequal opposite degrees orthogonal and (x,[u,v])=([x,u],v). Prove independence of both bracket expressions using the four-term Jacobi calculation of Kleshchev Theorem 2.2.3 and check invariance also in degrees N,-N,0. The radical is a graded ideal disjoint from h, hence zero. Conclude perfect opposite-root pairings, (alpha_i,alpha_j)=d_i a_ij, and [x_alpha,y_minusalpha]=(x,y)nu^{-1}(alpha). This proof precedes Serre generation.

contents.name: Kleshchev §9.1, pp.116--118
contents.support: Define weight modules with finite-dimensional weight spaces and support in finitely many sets lambda-Qplus; morphisms preserve the action. No finite generation or finite length is imposed. Finite positive-root degrees above a fixed weight imply restrictedness: if mu+beta<=lambda_j then beta has bounded nonnegative coordinates. Submodules and quotients inherit weight decompositions by finite interpolation.

contents.name: Kleshchev §9.1, pp.116--117
contents.support: Define b=h+nplus and M_A(lambda)=U(g) tensor over U(b) C_lambda, with nplus killing 1. The countable PBW lemma gives M as U(nminus) with a one-dimensional top and finite lower weight spaces. Include the unquotiented Mtilde used later. This is independent of the finite-dimensional published Verma theorem.

contents.name: Kleshchev §2.3, pp.32--34
contents.support: Restricted means g_alpha v=0 for all but finitely many positive roots for each v. Fix rho(h_i)=1. With dual Cartan bases u_a,u^a and opposite-root dual bases x_alpha,s and y_alpha,s, define Omega=2nu^{-1}(rho)+sum u_a u^a+2sum y_alpha,s x_alpha,s as an operator on restricted modules. The last sum is pointwise finite; each finite-dimensional canonical tensor is basis independent. No infinite element of U(g) is asserted.

contents.name: Kleshchev Lemma 2.3.1, Theorem 2.3.5 and Corollary 2.3.6, pp.32--36
contents.support: Pair the tensor identity sum y_alpha tensor [z,x_alpha]=sum [y_beta,z] tensor x_beta against each opposite tensor factor; invariance proves equality. For z=e_i telescope the two root-index sums in [Omega_0,z], leaving only the simple-root boundary; check z=f_i likewise and Cartan commutators directly. The boundary cancels the commutator of the finite Cartan term and 2nu^{-1}(rho). On a highest vector the positive factors vanish and the remaining scalar is (lambda+2rho,lambda); centrality propagates it to the generated module. No Serre or later representation theorem enters.

contents.name: Kleshchev §9.1, especially Lemma 9.1.3, pp.116--118
contents.support: A nonzero weight vector is primitive if its class is a nonzero highest vector modulo some submodule. It fails to be primitive precisely when it belongs to U(g)nplus v=U(nminus)U_0(nplus)v; prove this equality by PBW, including Cartan weights. In that event it is a finite sum of negative words applied to higher weight vectors. Induct on the finite set of support weights above the given weight to show that every vector is in the nminus-span of primitive vectors. No finite composition series is claimed.

contents.name: Kleshchev Lemmas 9.3.1--9.3.3, pp.122--124
contents.support: For countably spanned complex Lie algebras with supplied compatible ordered bases, first prove ker(U(g)->U(g/r))=rU(g) when r is an ideal, by inverse universal-property maps. For any Lie algebra l in this class, prove l intersect U_0(l)^2=[l,l]: one inclusion is xy-yx=[x,y], and the reverse follows by mapping to U(l/[l,l]), the symmetric algebra where degree-one and degree-at-least-two parts are disjoint. For a subalgebra r of g, order a basis of r before its complement. Let W be the vector span of the nonempty ordered monomials in the complement. PBW gives U(g)=U(r) direct-sum (U(r) tensor W) as a left U(r)-module, and U_0(g)=U_0(r) direct-sum (U(r) tensor W). Multiplying on the left by r gives rU_0(g)=U_0(r)^2 direct-sum (U_0(r) tensor W), because rU(r)=U_0(r) and rU_0(r)=U_0(r)^2 (both follow by expanding nonempty words in generators). Intersect with r, which lies in the first PBW summand, to obtain r intersect rU_0(g)=r intersect U_0(r)^2=[r,r]. Do not assert that ordered monomials of length at least two alone span rU_0(g): commutators can contribute degree-one basis vectors. For the finite-word graded applications choose compatible bases degree by degree by finite elimination; no unbased infinite-dimensional choice assertion is used.

contents.name: Kleshchev Proposition 9.3.4, pp.124--125
contents.support: Use the last-letter decomposition T(f_i)=C1 plus direct sum T(f_i)f_i, identifying Mtilde(0)prime with direct sum Mtilde(-alpha_i). After quotienting by r, identify the induced module with direct sum M(-alpha_i). The map a -> 1 tensor a v factors through rminus/[rminus,rminus]; use ASSOCIATIVE last-letter coefficients, not adjoint coefficients, to prove its kernel is rminus intersect rminus U_0(ntilde_minus)=[rminus,rminus]. Each summand has Casimir scalar zero since (alpha_i,alpha_i)=2(rho,alpha_i). Primitive generation gives relation generators in degrees alpha not simple satisfying (alpha,alpha)=2(rho,alpha). Lift from the abelianization by minimum-height induction: a nonzero positively graded quotient cannot equal its own commutator algebra. Check the actions explicitly before invoking the scalar.

contents.name: Kleshchev Lemma 3.1.1, §3.2 and Theorem 9.3.5 proof, pp.37--42, 125--126
contents.support: The Serre-vanishing lemma gives gbar->g. Serre relations imply ad e_i and ad f_i are locally nilpotent on every generator of gbar; the binomial derivation formula propagates this to all bracket words. Finite exponentials exp(ad f_i)exp(-ad e_i)exp(ad f_i) are automorphisms inducing s_i on h, both on gbar and g. They preserve kernel root multiplicities. If its positive part is nonzero take minimum height alpha; the generator constraint forces (alpha,alpha)=2(rho,alpha)>0. Since alpha is not simple, s_i alpha remains positive and minimality forces alpha(h_i)<=0 for every i; thus (alpha,alpha)=sum k_i d_i alpha(h_i)<=0. Contradiction. This Weyl argument does not use identification of the two quotients.

contents.name: Kleshchev §9.3, Theorem 9.3.5, pp.125--126
contents.support: Apply the preceding zero-residual-kernel lemma to both halves, using the sign-changing involution for the negative half. State precisely symmetrizable finite GCM over C; rplus and rminus are generated by their corresponding Serre elements. Triangular decomposition of the quotient and the PBW multiplication isomorphism then follow from the earlier Lie decomposition and the countable PBW lemma.

contents.name: Kleshchev §3.2, pp.40--42
contents.support: Define s_i(lambda)=lambda-lambda(h_i)alpha_i and W as their subgroup in GL(hstar); compute s_i^2=1 and the dual action s_i(h)=h-alpha_i(h)h_i. This definition precedes use of W in the residual-kernel proof.

contents.name: Kleshchev Lemma 3.2.3, pp.40--42
contents.support: For any GCM (no symmetrizability required), use Serre vanishing and the binomial derivation identity to construct the finite adjoint exponentials. Compute their action on h_i,e_i,f_i and on ker alpha_i in h; they send g_alpha bijectively to g_s_i(alpha), so multiplicity and roots are preserved. In the symmetrizable case compute form preservation directly from the reflection formula.

contents.name: Kleshchev §§5.1 and 5.3, pp.68--69, 73--74
contents.support: Define Delta_real=W Pi and Delta_imag=Delta minus Delta_real; retain positive and negative signs from the root lattice. The terms do not mean positive and negative squared length unless symmetrizability and the corresponding theorem have been proved.

contents.name: Kleshchev §5.1, pp.68--69; §3.2, pp.40--42
contents.support: Transport the simple triple (e_i,h_i,f_i) by a product of the proved automorphisms. It spans a copy of sl2 in degrees alpha,0,-alpha. Transporting the simple root space shows its dimension is one and no other nonzero scalar multiple of alpha is a root except +/-alpha. If the real coroot is named, check independence of the transporter by transporting [g_alpha,g_minusalpha] and imposing alpha(h_alpha)=2.

contents.name: Kleshchev §§4.1--4.2, pp.50--60
contents.support: Definition 4.1.1 gives the exact finite, affine and indefinite clauses: determinant/corank, the positive vector, and the respective nonnegative-cone condition. Theorem 4.1.12 makes them mutually exclusive and exhaustive for indecomposable GCMs, gives transpose invariance, and gives the unique affine positive null ray. Follow §§4.1.6--4.1.12: zero-coordinate propagation; split K_A={u:Au>=0} into the strictly positive cone or one-dimensional null-line cases; perturb zero coordinates of Au to strict positivity; use the strict linear alternative for the empty nonnegative cone. Theorem 4.2.3 supplies finite/affine symmetrizability. For B=DA symmetric, Proposition 4.2.1 gives the positive-definite finite, positive-semidefinite-corank-one affine, and indefinite signatures. The local expanded sum-of-squares identity supplies that signature route without importing an unlisted spectral theorem.

contents.name: Proposition 1.5.1 and Example 1.5.2, pp.20--21; Theorem 4.2.3, p.60
contents.support: The local finite-type trichotomy gives symmetrizability, a positive definite symmetrization and rank A=n, hence h=span(h_i). The root-descent lemma proves finite dimension. For each indecomposable component the simplicity lemma proves the associated algebra is nonabelian simple. Proposition 1.4.3 supplies the component direct-sum interface: zero off-diagonal blocks make the component generators commute, and the generator maps in both directions are inverse. The local symmetrizable Serre theorem gives the intrinsic universal Cartan--Serre presentation. The existing root decomposition, one-sign property and root descent identify the simple roots and their matrix alpha_j(h_i)=a_ij. No external finite-type presentation or classification theorem is used; the statements of simplicity and semisimplicity are explicit, so no radical criterion is silently imported.

contents.name: Example 1.5.2 (type A)
contents.support: For A=(2), no off-diagonal Serre relations exist. All brackets reduce to span e,f,h; E12,E21,diag(1,-1) give independent matrix images and all three sl2 brackets. Thus the universal algebra is exactly sl2.

contents.name: Example 1.5.2 specialized to A2
contents.support: For A2 write (ad e1)^2 e2=(ad e2)^2 e1=0 and both negative analogues. The positive half is spanned by e1,e2,[e1,e2], with independence witnessed by E12,E23,E13. Opposite matrices and diagonal coroots give the eight-dimensional sl3 model; verify the six nonzero roots and the row/coroot convention.

contents.name: Kleshchev Example 1.2.3 and Proposition 1.2.4, pp.10--12
contents.support: For [[2,-2],[-2,2]], n=2 and rank=1, hence dim h=3. Choose independent h0,h1,d and define alpha0=(2,-2,1), alpha1=(-2,2,0) in their dual coordinates. Verify independence and all four Cartan pairings; h0+h1 is killed by both roots.

contents.name: Kleshchev §4.1, pp.50--57 and Theorem 9.3.5, pp.125--126; explicit degree-(1,1) computation supplied locally
contents.support: For [[2,-3],[-3,2]], d1=d2=1, det=-5 and A(1,1)^t=(-1,-1)^t. The positive Lie degree (1,1) survives the Serre quotient because defining positive Serre generators have total degree 5; its nonzero bracket [e1,e2] has root alpha1+alpha2 of squared norm -2. All real roots have positive norm by form-preserving Weyl transport, so it is imaginary.

contents.name: Kleshchev Proposition 1.5.1, Lemma 1.5.3 and Example 1.5.4, pp.20--25; local adaptation to the sl3 loop model
contents.support: Use untwisted affine A2: all diagonal entries 2 and all off-diagonal entries -1. Give a self-contained loop-sl3 model C[t,t^-1] tensor sl3 plus Cc+Cd with central term m delta_m,-n tr(xy) and degree derivation. Check Jacobi by invariance of trace and m+n+k=0; take e0=tE31,e1=E12,e2=E23, opposite f0=t^-1 E13,f1=E21,f2=E32 and h0=c-E11+E33. Check generation using matrix commutators. The Cartan has dimension 4; each real root space is C t^m Eij and each m delta space (m!=0) is t^m times the two-dimensional traceless diagonal space. A nonzero ideal disjoint from Cartan has a homogeneous nonzero vector; bracket with the opposite matrix unit, or pair a nonzero diagonal against a diagonal using trace at degree -m, to obtain a nonzero Cartan element. Thus the model is the maximal-ideal quotient by the same recognition argument as Kleshchev 1.5.1. Since delta has norm zero, these are imaginary roots of multiplicity 2, for every nonzero m. This explicit verification avoids a forbidden forward dependency on RL-13.

contents.name: Kleshchev Lemma 1.3.2 and Theorem 1.3.3, pp.13--16
contents.support: Finite Vandermonde projections onto weight spaces.

contents.name: Lemma 1.4.5
contents.support: Use finite weight interpolation to reduce to a weight component. Its span under iterated ad h and ad e_i stays in nplus and is stable under every ad f_i by Jacobi and the defining relations. It is therefore an ideal disjoint from h and vanishes by maximality. Apply the sign-changing involution for the other half.

contents.name: Lemma 3.1.1
contents.support: Derive [e,f^m]=m f^(m-1)(h-m+1) by induction. Apply to v=f_j of i-weight -a_ij. The putative Serre vector is killed by e_i, by every e_k outside i,j, and by e_j using a_ij=0 iff a_ji=0 in the boundary case. The opposite-simple-centralizer lemma kills it. This proves vanishing only; generation waits for the Casimir relation-module proof.

contents.name: Lemma 4.1.4 and Proposition 4.1.5
contents.support: Minimize the squared Euclidean norm on the finite convex hull. It is closed and bounded (derive compactness from the finite simplex and its continuous linear image); the hypothesis excludes zero. For a minimum x, expand ||x+t(y-x)||^2 and divide by t>0 to get (x,y)>=||x||^2>0. The reverse implication follows by pairing with x. Apply to rows of -C and standard coordinate rows for the consequence. This external compactness supplier needs its transitive proof audit before readiness.

contents.name: Section 1.3 proof: free Lie algebra in its tensor algebra
contents.support: First construct the abstract bracket-word quotient, which has the universal property by recursive evaluation and is countably spanned. The universal properties give inverse associative maps between its enveloping algebra and the tensor algebra. PBW injectivity embeds the abstract free Lie algebra into the tensor algebra; its image is the Lie subalgebra generated by the letters. This avoids assuming freeness from a concrete subalgebra before its universal property is proved.

contents.name: Section 9.1: PBW freeness on the highest vector
contents.support: Section 9.1 uses PBW for its Verma modules; it does not supply the full local countable-basis proof. The proposed finite-rewriting/Jacobi proof is in the manifest. Its independent source/transitive semantic audit remains an explicit readiness obligation.

contents.name: Sections 1.3--1.4, pp.13--19: Q-grading and height
contents.support: Specify Qplus contains zero; roots themselves exclude zero. The simple-root independence makes both coordinates and the height unambiguous.

contents.name: Proposition 1.4.3, pp.17--18: direct sums
contents.support: The local finite-type trichotomy gives symmetrizability, a positive definite symmetrization and rank A=n, hence h=span(h_i). The root-descent lemma proves finite dimension. For each indecomposable component the simplicity lemma proves the associated algebra is nonabelian simple. Proposition 1.4.3 supplies the component direct-sum interface: zero off-diagonal blocks make the component generators commute, and the generator maps in both directions are inverse. The local symmetrizable Serre theorem gives the intrinsic universal Cartan--Serre presentation. The existing root decomposition, one-sign property and root descent identify the simple roots and their matrix alpha_j(h_i)=a_ij. No external finite-type presentation or classification theorem is used; the statements of simplicity and semisimplicity are explicit, so no radical criterion is silently imported.

contents.name: Kleshchev §§2.1--2.2, Theorem 2.2.3, pp.26--32
contents.support: The Cartan radical calculation is included in the invariant-form proof.

contents.name: Lemma 1.4.7 and Proposition 1.4.8(ii): remaining connected-support and general ideal structure
contents.reason: Nonsingular indecomposable simplicity from Proposition 1.4.8(i) is now proved locally; remaining ideal-structure clauses stay in the affine programme.

contents.name: Section 3.3 Coxeter presentation and Section 3.4 Tits cone
contents.reason: The Serre proof needs only simple-reflection automorphisms and root signs, not the Coxeter or Tits-cone theorems.

contents.name: Propositions 3.1.4--3.1.5 integrable module decomposition and strings
contents.reason: General integrable-module strings belong to the integrable module supplier; the present adjoint exponential calculation is direct.

contents.name: Proposition 9.1.2 simple highest-weight quotient
contents.reason: The unique simple quotient is owned by RL-14; relation modules here need only Verma PBW and primitive vectors.

contents.name: Section 5.2 real-root coordinate classification
contents.reason: Detailed finite/affine coordinate root lists are not needed for the definition or one-dimensional real-root theorem.

contents.name: Lemma 5.3.2 and Theorem 5.3.3 fundamental imaginary cone
contents.reason: The full imaginary-cone classification requires additional root-string and support arguments; preserve it for the character-theory development.

contents.name: Propositions 5.3.4--5.3.6 imaginary multiples and isotropic support
contents.reason: General imaginary-root multiples and isotropic support require the affine-root development; the explicit affine A2 witness is proved directly here.

contents.name: Kleshchev Proposition 4.3.2, printed pp.63–64, complete proof read; local height descent and dual-basis lattice bound replace its compact-group route
contents.support: Work componentwise with the positive definite symmetrization B=DA proved by the local trichotomy, using (alpha_i,alpha_j)=d_i a_ij. For a positive root beta=sum m_i alpha_i, positivity of (beta,beta)=sum m_i(alpha_i,beta) gives i with (alpha_i,beta)>0. Thus beta(h_i)>0 is an integer. If beta is not simple, its support contains an index different from i: the local root-space result excludes pure multiples k alpha_i with k>1. The reflected root s_i beta=beta-beta(h_i)alpha_i retains a positive coefficient at that different index. The proved one-sign root decomposition and Weyl root invariance therefore make it positive, and its height is smaller. Induction on the positive integer height reaches a simple root. Negative roots follow by sign and the simple reflection of alpha_i to -alpha_i. Weyl form invariance implies every root has squared length in the finite set {2d_i}. To prove finiteness without a compact-orthogonal-group theorem, let v_i be the basis dual to the alpha_i for the positive form. Cauchy–Schwarz follows directly by minimizing (u-t v,u-t v) over real t. Hence each integer root coefficient satisfies |m_i|^2=|(beta,v_i)|^2<=C(v_i,v_i), where C=max_i 2d_i. Only finitely many integer coefficient tuples meet these finitely many fixed bounds. Existence of the dual basis follows by finite Gaussian elimination since positivity makes B invertible. Weyl transport preserves the one-dimensional simple root spaces. Finally the existing triangular weight decomposition is h plus the root spaces, and dim h=n because A is invertible. Thus dim g=n+|Delta| is finite. No classification, root-string completeness, highest-root theorem, recurrence or external Serre existence theorem is assumed.

contents.name: Kleshchev Proposition 1.4.8(i), printed pp.19–20, complete simplicity argument read
contents.support: By the maximal-ideal quotient construction, every nonzero ideal J of g intersects h nontrivially: its inverse image would otherwise be an ideal disjoint from h larger than the defining maximal one. Let 0!=h in J intersect h. Since A is nonsingular, the n independent simple roots form a basis of h-star (dim h=n), so alpha_i(h)!=0 for some i. Then [h,e_i]=alpha_i(h)e_i puts e_i in J, [e_i,f_i]=h_i puts h_i in J, and [h_i,f_i]=-2f_i puts f_i in J. If a_ij!=0, [h_i,e_j]=a_ij e_j puts e_j in J, hence also h_j and f_j. The graph whose edges are nonzero off-diagonal entries is connected by indecomposability, so a finite path repeats this argument at every index. The h_i span h because A is nonsingular. All defining generators lie in J, so J=g. The simple sl2 triple is nonzero by Cartan injectivity and the root-space construction, showing g is nonabelian. This proves simplicity directly rather than invoking a classification or a radical theorem.

contents.name: Lemma 4.2.9: indecomposable matrix has connected nonzero-entry graph
contents.support: Used in the simplicity proof. Partition the finite indices by paths of nonzero off-diagonal entries. Distinct classes have zero entries between them, and conversely a block decomposition disconnects the graph. Thus indecomposability is equivalent to connectedness. This finite equivalence is proved inline, not deferred.

contents.name: Proposition 4.2.10: nonsingular indecomposable simplicity clause
contents.support: The owned maximal-disjoint-ideal proof gives Cartan intersection, then nonsingularity and the connected nonzero-entry graph propagate a nonzero ideal through every generator. The singular/general ideal-structure clauses remain separately deferred.
